groups.instructionTh: ฟังบทสนทนา แล้วตอบคำถามข้อละ 1 คำตอบ
groups.title: Two internship offers

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Thanks for seeing me at such short notice. I've got two internship offers, and I have to give both companies an answer by Friday.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: That's a nice problem to have. Tell me about them.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: The first is with Larkspur Analytics, the big data consultancy in Bangkok. It's paid, it's well known, and it would look great on my CV.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: And the second?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: It's with a small start-up called Tidewell that builds water-monitoring sensors for farms. It's unpaid for the first month, but they've said I'd be working directly with the engineering team.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: What did the people at Larkspur say you would actually be doing day to day?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: That's the odd thing. The interview was mostly about the company's reputation. When I asked about my tasks, they were rather vague, something about "supporting client projects."

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: That's worth noticing. In my experience, large firms sometimes treat interns as an extra pair of hands for photocopying and data entry. That's not always the case, of course, but vague answers are a yellow flag.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: So you think I should go with the start-up?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: I didn't say that. I think you should find out more before you decide. Could you email Larkspur and ask to speak to a current or former intern?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: I hadn't thought of that. But what about the money? Going a whole month without pay would be tough.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Then ask Tidewell whether they'd cover your travel costs during that month. Small companies often have more flexibility than you'd expect, but they won't offer unless you ask.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: All right. And if both answers turn out to be disappointing?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Then think about which one will teach you something you can't learn in a lecture hall. In the long run, the name on your CV matters far less than what you can say you actually did.

items.stem: Why has the woman come to see the man?

To complain about an interview
To get advice on two internships
To ask for more time to finish an assignment
items.explanationTh: ผู้หญิงบอกตั้งแต่ต้นว่า "I've got two internship offers" และต้องตอบบริษัทภายในวันศุกร์ จึงมาขอคำแนะนำในการเลือกระหว่างสองที่

items.stem: What does the man mean when he calls vague answers "a yellow flag"?

They are normal and can safely be ignored.
They show that the interviewer was nervous.
items.explanationTh: "yellow flag" คือสัญญาณเตือนระดับกลาง เขาบอกว่า "That's not always the case" และแนะนำให้หาข้อมูลเพิ่ม จึงไม่ได้หมายความว่าบริษัทไม่ซื่อสัตย์แน่นอน แต่ควรตรวจสอบ

items.explanationTh: ผู้ชายแนะนำว่า "ask Tidewell whether they'd cover your travel costs during that month" คือให้ถามเรื่องค่าเดินทางในเดือนแรกที่ไม่มีค่าตอบแทน

groups.instructionTh: ฟังบทสนทนา แล้วตอบคำถามข้อละ 1 คำตอบ
groups.title: A change to the exam timetable

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Did you see the email from the faculty office? The Organic Chemistry final has been postponed.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Postponed? Until when? I've been cramming all week for Monday.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: They haven't fixed a new date yet. Apparently the exam hall in the Sirindra Building failed its fire-safety inspection, and they can't use it until the alarm system's been replaced.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Couldn't they just move us to another room?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: That's what I wondered, but there are over three hundred of us, and every other hall that size is already booked for other finals.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Typical. So we're just left hanging?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Not entirely. The email said the new date will be announced by Wednesday, and it'll be no earlier than the following Monday.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Well, at least that gives me another week. I'm actually a bit behind on reaction mechanisms, so maybe it's a blessing in disguise.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Lucky you. For me it could be a disaster. I'm flying home to Hat Yai on the twentieth for my sister's graduation, and if the exam ends up on the twenty-first, I'm stuck.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Did the email say anything about students with conflicts?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Yes, there's a form for requesting an alternative sitting. But it has to be submitted within forty-eight hours of the new date being announced, along with some kind of supporting evidence.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Then I'd keep your flight confirmation handy. And maybe email Dr. Pimchanok now, so she knows the situation before the date is even set.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Good idea. I'd rather raise it early than look as if I'm making excuses at the last minute.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Exactly. And in the meantime, do you want to go over the mechanisms together? We've both got time on our hands now.

items.stem: Why has the exam been postponed?
options: Too many students registered for the course.
The lecturer is unavailable on Monday.
Its venue did not pass a safety inspection.
The exam paper has to be rewritten.
items.explanationTh: ผู้ชายบอกว่าห้องสอบ "failed its fire-safety inspection" และใช้ไม่ได้จนกว่าจะเปลี่ยนระบบเตือนไฟ จำนวนนักศึกษา 300 คนเป็นเหตุผลที่ย้ายห้องไม่ได้ ไม่ใช่สาเหตุของการเลื่อน

items.stem: Why can the exam not simply be held in a different room?
options: The faculty office is closed for the week.
The other rooms also lack working alarms.
The students voted against changing rooms.
No other room of a suitable size is free.
items.explanationTh: ผู้ชายอธิบายว่ามีนักศึกษากว่า 300 คน และ "every other hall that size is already booked" จึงไม่มีห้องขนาดพอที่ว่าง

items.stem: How does the woman feel about the postponement?
options: She sees it as a chance to catch up on her studies.
She is annoyed because it ruins her travel plans.
She does not care when the exam takes place.
She is worried that she will forget what she learned.
items.explanationTh: เธอบอกว่ายังตามเรื่อง reaction mechanisms ไม่ทัน และ "maybe it's a blessing in disguise" คือเรื่องที่ดูแย่แต่กลับเป็นผลดี ส่วนคนที่มีปัญหาเรื่องการเดินทางคือผู้ชาย

items.stem: What must the man do to request an alternative sitting?
options: Send in a form and evidence within two days of the announcement
Send in a form and evidence before the new date is announced
Persuade the lecturer to change the date for the whole class
Show his flight booking to the faculty office on the morning of the exam
items.explanationTh: ผู้ชายบอกว่าแบบฟอร์มต้องส่ง "within forty-eight hours of the new date being announced" พร้อมหลักฐาน คือภายในสองวันหลังประกาศ ไม่ใช่ก่อนประกาศ

items.stem: Why does the man agree to contact Dr. Pimchanok straight away?
options: Early notice will make his request more believable.
He wants help with his revision.
He needs her signature on his flight booking.
He hopes she will postpone the exam once again.
items.explanationTh: เขาบอกว่า "I'd rather raise it early than look as if I'm making excuses at the last minute" จึงอยากแจ้งล่วงหน้าเพื่อไม่ให้ดูเหมือนข้ออ้างนาทีสุดท้าย

groups.instructionTh: ฟังการบรรยาย แล้วตอบคำถามข้อละ 1 คำตอบ
groups.title: Lecture: the economics of streaming
groups.text:
Good morning, everyone. Today I want to look at a business that most of you use every day without ever thinking about its economics: music and video streaming.

Let's begin with a puzzle. A streaming service may have tens of millions of subscribers, yet for years many such companies reported losses. How is that possible? The answer lies in the structure of their costs. A streaming platform pays in two main ways: a large fixed cost to build and maintain its technology, and a royalty to rights holders that grows with every single play. In other words, the more popular the service becomes, the more it owes. Growth alone does not guarantee profit.

This brings us to what is called the pro-rata model. Under this system, all subscription money is pooled and then divided according to each artist's share of total plays. It sounds fair, but consider a listener who pays her monthly fee and listens only to a little-known jazz trio. Most of her money doesn't go to that trio at all. It goes to whichever stars dominate everyone else's playlists. Some economists have therefore proposed a user-centric model, in which each subscriber's fee is split only among the artists that subscriber actually played.

Last year, a study by the Halvorsen Institute modelled what would happen if one mid-sized platform switched to the user-centric approach. The headline result was surprisingly modest. The very top artists lost around four percent of their income, while niche performers gained a little more than that. So it is hardly a revolution. But for a small band, a few extra percent might be the difference between touring and giving up.

Finally, notice that platforms are increasingly producing their own content. Why? Because if you own the series or the recording, you pay no royalties on it. Keep that in mind when you read this week's case study, because it explains a great deal about which shows end up being promoted on your home screen.

items.stem: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why physical albums are more profitable than streams
What students need to do to start a streaming company
How recorded music developed over the last century
How streaming services earn and share out money
items.explanationTh: ผู้บรรยายเปิดว่าจะพูดถึง "its economics" ของบริการสตรีมมิง แล้วอธิบายโครงสร้างต้นทุน ค่าลิขสิทธิ์ และวิธีแบ่งเงินให้ศิลปิน จึงเป็นเรื่องการหาเงินและแบ่งเงินของบริการสตรีมมิง

items.stem: According to the speaker, why can a popular streaming service still lose money?
options: Its subscribers tend to cancel after one month.
It must pay a fee for every album it stores.
Its technology becomes cheaper far too slowly to help.
Its royalty payments rise as people use it more.
items.explanationTh: ผู้บรรยายบอกว่าค่าลิขสิทธิ์ "grows with every single play" และ "the more popular the service becomes, the more it owes" จึงขาดทุนได้แม้มีผู้ใช้มาก

items.stem: What point does the speaker make with the example of the jazz listener?
options: Fans of niche music should pay a higher monthly fee.
Small bands earn more under the pro-rata model.
Jazz is steadily losing listeners on streaming platforms.
Under the pro-rata model, her fee mostly goes to stars.
items.explanationTh: ตัวอย่างนี้แสดงว่าในระบบ pro-rata เงินของผู้ฟังส่วนใหญ่ "goes to whichever stars dominate everyone else's playlists" ไม่ได้ไปถึงวงที่เธอฟังจริง

items.stem: What did the Halvorsen Institute study find?
options: A user-centric model would change artist income only slightly.
The platform would lose subscribers after switching.
Niche performers would earn less than they do at present.
Top artists would lose nearly half of their income.
items.explanationTh: ผลการศึกษา "surprisingly modest" ศิลปินระดับท็อปเสียรายได้ราว 4% และศิลปินกลุ่มเฉพาะได้เพิ่มเล็กน้อย ผู้บรรยายสรุปว่า "hardly a revolution"

items.stem: What does the speaker imply about content that platforms produce themselves?
options: Platforms may promote it since it costs no royalties.
It is usually shown only to brand-new subscribers.

groups.title: Lecture: who decided what time it is?
groups.text:
Before we turn to next week's reading, I'd like to spend a few minutes on a question that sounds almost silly: who decided what time it is?

For most of human history, time was local. Each town set its clocks by the sun, so noon was simply the moment when the sun stood highest in the sky. Because the sun appears to travel from east to west, a town even a short distance to the west would be a few minutes behind its neighbour. Nobody minded, since almost nobody travelled fast enough to notice.

The railway changed all that. Once trains could cross a country in a matter of hours, dozens of local times became a genuine headache. A timetable printed in one city might be wrong by ten or fifteen minutes in the next, and on a line where trains in both directions shared a single track, a misread timetable was not merely inconvenient. It could put two trains on the same stretch of rail at the same moment. So it was railway companies, rather than governments, that first adopted a single standard time along their routes.

What interests me as a historian is the resistance. In a number of towns, people refused to accept railway time as the real time. Some public clocks were even fitted with two minute hands, one showing local solar time and the other showing the railway's time. To many residents, giving up local time felt like handing a piece of their town's identity over to a distant company.

Eventually, of course, standard time won, and later the world was divided into time zones. But the debate reminds us that technical standards are never purely technical. They decide whose convenience counts. When you read Chapter Six, I'd like you to look for a modern example of the same tension, perhaps in the way online services choose default languages or date formats for their users.

groups.title: The universe's missing mass
groups.text:
When astronomers first measured how quickly stars orbit the centres of their galaxies, they expected the results to follow a familiar rule. In our own solar system, distant planets move more slowly than those close to the sun, because the sun's gravitational pull weakens with distance. Galaxies, it was assumed, would behave in much the same way: stars near the bright, crowded core should race around quickly, while those in the dim outskirts should drift along at a more leisurely pace.

That is not what the measurements showed. Again and again, stars far from the centre were found to be moving roughly as fast as those much closer in. If the visible matter in these galaxies were all there was, the outer stars would be travelling fast enough to escape altogether, and the galaxies would long ago have flown apart. Something was holding them together, and whatever it was, it could not be seen.

The name given to this invisible something is dark matter. The term is, in a sense, a confession of ignorance. Dark matter does not emit, absorb or reflect light in any way that current instruments can detect; it reveals itself only through its gravity. Yet the indirect evidence for it is now considerable. Beyond the rotation of galaxies, astronomers point to the way light from distant galaxies is bent as it passes massive clusters, an effect known as gravitational lensing. The amount of bending is often far greater than the visible matter in a cluster could produce. Calculations based on such observations suggest that ordinary matter (everything made of atoms, from stars to the human body) accounts for only around a sixth of all the matter in the universe.

What dark matter actually is remains one of the great open questions in physics. For several decades, a leading candidate has been a class of hypothetical particles that interact with ordinary matter only extremely weakly. Detectors have been built deep underground, shielded from cosmic radiation, in the hope of catching one of these particles in a rare collision with an atomic nucleus. So far, these experiments have produced no convincing signal. Each null result narrows the range of possibilities, but it also feeds a growing unease.

That unease has given new energy to a rival school of thought. Rather than adding an unseen substance to the universe, some theorists propose that our understanding of gravity itself is incomplete, and that at the very low accelerations found at the edges of galaxies, gravity behaves differently from what established theory predicts. Such modified-gravity theories can reproduce the rotation of galaxies with impressive economy. Their weakness is that they struggle to explain other observations, notably certain collisions between galaxy clusters in which the gravitational effects appear to be separated from the visible gas, exactly as if an invisible mass had passed straight through.

Dr. Ilse Varnholt of the Kessington Observatory compares the situation to a detective story in which the culprit has left footprints everywhere but has never been seen. "It would be strange," she says, "to conclude that footprints can appear by themselves. But it would be equally foolish to arrest someone before we know who they are."

groups.title: Why sensible minds go astray
groups.text:
Ask a room full of people whether they drive more carefully than the average motorist, and most hands will go up. Not everyone in the room can be right, of course, but nobody is lying, either. Each person is drawing on a mind that, for reasons which once served our ancestors well, tends to see itself in a flattering light. Psychologists call such systematic distortions in judgement cognitive biases, and over the past half-century they have catalogued dozens of them.

It is worth stressing what a bias is not. It is not simply a mistake. Random errors scatter in all directions and tend to cancel one another out when many judgements are averaged. Biases, by contrast, push our thinking consistently in one direction, which is precisely why they are so hard to notice and so costly when they go uncorrected.

Consider confirmation bias, perhaps the best known of all. Once we hold a belief, we tend to seek out, remember and give extra weight to information that supports it, while treating contrary evidence with suspicion. In a study at the Marlowe Institute, volunteers who held opposing views on a proposed city transport scheme were shown the same mixed set of research findings. Afterwards, both groups reported that the evidence had strengthened their original position. The information was identical; what differed was how each side processed it.

A second example is anchoring. When people are asked to estimate an unknown quantity, their answers are pulled towards whatever number they happened to encounter beforehand, even when that number is plainly irrelevant. In one classroom demonstration, students first wrote down the last two digits of their phone number and then guessed the price of a used bicycle. Those with high digits offered noticeably higher prices. Nobody believed that a phone number had anything to do with bicycles, yet the number left its mark.

Why would evolution produce minds that work like this? One influential answer is that biases are side effects of mental shortcuts, or heuristics, which allow us to make fast decisions with limited information. For an early human deciding whether a rustle in the grass was a predator, speed mattered far more than statistical precision. A shortcut that was occasionally wrong but usually quick may have been a better bet than careful reasoning that arrived too late.

The practical question is whether we can do better, and here the evidence is sobering. Simply teaching people about biases appears to have only a limited effect: in one experiment, participants who could define confirmation bias perfectly went on to display it in the very next task. More promising are changes to the setting in which decisions are made. Some hospitals and engineering firms now require teams to list the reasons a preferred plan might fail before approving it. Such procedures do not make individuals any less biased, but they create structures in which one person's blind spot is more likely to be caught by someone else.

In the end, the realistic goal is not to eliminate biases, which may well be impossible, but to recognise the situations in which they are most likely to lead us astray.

groups.title: When reefs turn white
groups.text:
Seen from a boat, a healthy coral reef can look like a garden of colourful rock. In fact, each coral is a colony of tiny animals called polyps, and much of its colour comes from microscopic algae living inside their tissues. The relationship between the two is a remarkable partnership. The algae, sheltered within the coral, use sunlight to produce sugars through photosynthesis, and they pass a large share of this food to their hosts. In return, the coral provides the algae with a protected home and with the carbon dioxide and nutrients they need. For many reef-building corals, the algae supply most of their energy.

Coral bleaching occurs when this partnership breaks down. When the surrounding water stays unusually warm for an extended period, the algae's photosynthetic machinery is damaged and begins to produce harmful by-products. The coral responds by expelling the algae. Without them, the coral's tissue becomes almost transparent, revealing the white limestone skeleton underneath; hence the term "bleaching".

A bleached coral is not necessarily a dead one. It is better thought of as a starving one. If temperatures return to normal within a few weeks, the coral can take in new algae from the water and gradually recover its colour. If the heat persists, however, the coral is likely to die, and the reef that depends on it begins to decline. Fish that feed or shelter among the coral move away or disappear, and the structure itself, no longer maintained by living polyps, is slowly worn down by waves and burrowing organisms.

Historically, mass bleaching events were rare, and reefs had years or even decades to recover between them. Researchers at the Tamarind Bay Marine Laboratory, who have photographed the same twenty reef sites every year for three decades, report that the interval between major events at their sites has shrunk from an average of roughly eighteen years to fewer than six. "Recovery is still happening," notes the laboratory's director, Dr. Sunee Rattanakorn, "but the reefs are being asked to run a marathon while someone keeps moving the finish line."

Not all corals respond in the same way. Some species, and even some individual colonies within a species, tolerate heat far better than others. Part of this difference seems to depend on which type of algae a coral hosts, since certain types are more heat-resistant. This has led some scientists to explore what is known as assisted evolution: selectively breeding heat-tolerant corals in laboratories, or encouraging corals to host tougher algae, before transplanting them onto damaged reefs.

Such projects attract both enthusiasm and caution. Supporters argue that they could buy valuable time. Critics point out that reefs are vast, whereas laboratory work can only ever restore small patches. They also fear that the promise of a technical fix could weaken the pressure to deal with the warming ocean itself. Most researchers, Dr. Rattanakorn included, regard assisted evolution as a supplement to, rather than a substitute for, tackling the underlying causes of rising sea temperatures.

groups.title: Print, pixels and the lessons of history
groups.text:
Whenever a new communication technology appears, commentators reach for historical comparisons, and none is more popular than the printing press. The internet, we are often told, is the most important information revolution since movable type made books cheap enough to spread across Europe in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. The comparison is useful, but only if it is handled with care.

The similarities are real. Before printing, books were copied by hand, a slow and costly process that kept written knowledge in the hands of a small number of institutions. Printing broke that bottleneck. Within a few generations, the number of books in circulation had multiplied many times over, and readers could compare texts in ways that had previously been all but impossible. The internet has had a comparable effect on the cost of publishing: today anyone with a connection can address a potential audience of millions at almost no expense.

Both technologies also produced a flood of material of very uneven quality. Historians of print note that alongside scholarly works came cheap pamphlets full of rumour, exaggeration and deliberate falsehood. Critics at the time complained that there were simply too many books for anyone to read and no reliable way to tell the good from the bad. Such complaints sound strikingly familiar to anyone who has scrolled through a social media feed.

Yet the differences are at least as instructive. The first is speed. A printed pamphlet took days or weeks to travel from one city to the next; a post online can circle the globe in minutes. Printing societies therefore had time, however imperfectly, to develop institutions for sorting reliable information from unreliable: publishers who staked their reputations on what they printed, reviewers, libraries and, eventually, formal systems of academic peer review. These institutions took well over a century to mature. It is far from clear that the internet will grant us the same breathing space.

The second difference concerns who controls distribution. A printed book, once sold, belonged to its reader, and no one could quietly change which pages that reader saw. Online, by contrast, much of what we encounter is selected by ranking systems designed by a small number of companies, often with the aim of holding our attention rather than informing us. In this respect, argues the historian Dr. Marcus Ellery, the internet may be less like the printing press than like a vast bookshop in which the shelves are rearranged for every customer who walks in.

None of this means that the comparison should be abandoned. Its real value lies less in predicting outcomes than in reminding us that the effects of a technology are shaped by the institutions and habits that grow up around it. The printing press did not, by itself, produce either the scientific journal or the propaganda pamphlet; people built both. The same will be true of whatever the internet eventually becomes.

groups.title: The minimum wage: an argument that will not go away
groups.text:
Few economic policies provoke as much argument as the minimum wage. To its supporters, a legal wage floor is a simple matter of fairness: no one who works full-time should be unable to cover basic living costs. To its critics, it is a well-meaning policy that risks harming the very people it is intended to help. What makes the debate so durable is that both sides can point to evidence, and that the evidence is genuinely harder to interpret than either side tends to admit.

The traditional case against the minimum wage rests on a basic model of supply and demand. If the government sets the price of labour above the level the market would produce, employers will buy less of it. Some workers, typically the least experienced, will therefore be priced out of jobs altogether. On this view, a worker who earns nothing at a higher legal wage is worse off than one who earned a little at a lower market wage.

For decades, many economists regarded this argument as close to settled. That changed when researchers began comparing neighbouring regions that had adopted different minimum wages at the same time. If the basic model were correct, employment in low-wage industries should have fallen in the regions that raised their minimum. In a number of such studies, it did not fall noticeably, and in some it even rose slightly.

Several explanations have been offered. One is that, in many local labour markets, employers have more power to set wages than the simple model assumes, especially where there are few alternative employers. Under such conditions, a modest minimum wage can raise pay without reducing jobs, and may even draw more people into work. Another is that higher pay reduces the costly turnover of staff: workers who are paid better tend to stay longer, sparing employers the expense of constant recruitment and training.

None of this means that the minimum wage can be raised without limit. Even economists sympathetic to the policy accept that, at some point, a sufficiently high minimum would lead employers to cut staff, reduce hours or replace workers with machines. The real disagreement is about where that point lies, and it may well lie in different places in different economies. A wage floor that is harmless in a prosperous capital city could be damaging in a rural province where living costs and typical wages are much lower.

For this reason, some governments set minimum wages that vary by region, and a number of them link the rate to a fixed percentage of the local median wage rather than to a single national figure. Economists at the Valmora Policy Centre, for example, recommend reviewing the rate every year against local data rather than raising it in large, infrequent steps. Such approaches will not end the argument, but they reflect a broader shift in the debate: away from whether a minimum wage is good or bad in principle, and towards how it can be set sensibly in practice.
